heading: Cold open
narration: Earth's longest mountain range was built without a single collision. A mid-ocean ridge forms where two tectonic plates are pulled apart: the mantle beneath rises to fill the gap, melts as its pressure drops, and erupts as fresh basalt that cools into new ocean crust.

args.caption: A continuous range of underwater volcanoes

heading: Cold open
narration: NOAA describes the result as a continuous range of underwater volcanoes stretching nearly 65,000 kilometres around the globe, like the seams on a baseball.

heading: Cold open
narration: That figure tells you how big the system is. It does not tell you why rock rises, why it melts without being heated, or why the ridge stands tall at all.

args.caption: A continuous range of underwater volcanoes

heading: Cold open
narration: And it hides an older assumption that this evidence overturned: that mountains are what you get when the crust is squeezed. This one is what you get when it is stretched.

heading: Title card
narration: How is a mid-ocean ridge formed?

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: Start with what a mid-ocean ridge is not. The Alps and the Himalayas are folds, crust crumpled and stacked where plates converge.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: A mid-ocean ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: Along its crest, two plates move away from each other, and the gap between them never stays open.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: Something from below always arrives to close it. The ridge is the shape that filling takes.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: That changes how you should picture the process. It is tempting to imagine molten rock forcing its way upward and shoving the plates aside, like a wedge driven into a log.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: The mainstream view, which you will find in the plate tectonics material published by USGS, runs mostly the other way.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: The plates are pulled apart by forces acting elsewhere, chiefly the weight of old, cold plate sinking back into the mantle at subduction zones, often thousands of kilometres from the ridge.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: The ridge responds to that pull. It is less an engine than an opening that keeps healing.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: Here is the sequence, in short form: plates pulled apart, mantle rises, rock melts, basalt erupts.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: The mantle beneath the crest rises passively into the space the plates leave behind.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: As it rises, some of that rock melts. The melt, lighter than the solid rock around it, collects and climbs.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: It erupts onto the seafloor or freezes just beneath it, and the cooled basalt becomes new ocean crust, welded onto the trailing edges of both plates.

heading: The ridge is a crack being filled, not a fold being pushed up
narration: Then the plates keep moving, and the cycle begins again on the same seam.

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: The step that surprises most people is the melting. The mantle beneath a ridge is mostly solid rock.

args.meaning: rock melting because the pressure on it drops
args.boundary: not melting caused by added heat

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: It is extremely hot, but it is also under enormous pressure, and pressure raises the temperature at which rock melts.

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: Hold that rock deep down and it stays solid. Let it rise, and the pressure on it falls faster than the rock can lose its heat.

args.meaning: rock melting because the pressure on it drops
args.boundary: not melting caused by added heat

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: At some point it crosses its own melting point without any heat being added at all.

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: Geologists call this decompression melting: rock melting because the pressure on it drops, not melting caused by added heat.

args.meaning: rock melting because the pressure on it drops
args.boundary: not melting caused by added heat

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: Nobody can watch this happen, so it is inferred from three lines of evidence.

args.title: How melting is inferred
args.conclusion: the mantle partly melts as it rises

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: First, lab experiments on mantle rock squeeze and heat samples to map the conditions where they begin to melt.

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: Second, the composition of ridge basalt, dredged and drilled from the seafloor, matches what partial melting of mantle rock should produce.

args.title: How melting is inferred
args.conclusion: the mantle partly melts as it rises

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: Only a fraction of the rock melts, and that melt carries a recognisable chemical signature.

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: Third, seismic images beneath ridges show zones where sound waves slow down, which is what you would expect where some melt is present.

args.title: How melting is inferred
args.conclusion: the mantle partly melts as it rises

heading: The mantle melts because pressure falls, not because it heats up
narration: None of these alone proves the process. Together they point the same way: the mantle partly melts as it rises.

heading: Producer POV
narration: The ocean, the interior of the planet, underground ecosystems, even parts of our own bodies. We live inside systems we cannot fully explain.

args.text: The ocean, the interior of the planet, underground ecosystems, even parts of our own bodies. We live inside systems we cannot fully explain.

heading: The ridge stands tall because its rock is young
narration: Now the height. If nothing is being squeezed, it is fair to wonder why there is a mountain range at all.

includes: hot rock taking up more room

heading: The ridge stands tall because its rock is young
narration: The answer is temperature. Freshly made crust, and the mantle just beneath it, are hot, and hot rock takes up more room than the same rock cold.

heading: The ridge stands tall because its rock is young
narration: So the newest seafloor rides high. As the plates carry it away from the crest, it cools, contracts and grows denser, and it settles lower over millions of years.

includes: hot rock taking up more room

heading: The ridge stands tall because its rock is young
narration: The ridge is a long, broad swell of warm, young rock, sloping down on either side into the older, colder, deeper floor of the abyss.

heading: The ridge stands tall because its rock is young
narration: Its height is hot rock taking up more room, not rock piled up by force.

includes: hot rock taking up more room

heading: The ridge stands tall because its rock is young
narration: That explanation has a consequence you can test. If the height comes from cooling, then seafloor depth should track seafloor age in a predictable way: shallow at the crest, deeper with distance, and flattening out as the rock approaches the temperature of its surroundings.

heading: The ridge stands tall because its rock is young
narration: Depth surveys across the major ocean basins show broadly that pattern. It is one of the quieter confirmations that the ridge is a thermal feature, not a structural one.

heading: The first clue was a valley nobody expected
narration: The modern story begins with maps. In the years after the Second World War, research ships crossed the Atlantic running echo sounders, timing sound pulses to the seafloor and back to measure depth.

args.title: Mapping the Atlantic floor
args.conclusion: a rift where the crust splits

heading: The first clue was a valley nobody expected
narration: Marie Tharp, working with the geologist Bruce Heezen, turned those echo-sounding depth profiles into hand-drawn cross-sections of the ocean floor.

heading: The first clue was a valley nobody expected
narration: Lined up side by side, the profiles showed something consistent: a valley along the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, running down its centre like a notch.

args.title: Mapping the Atlantic floor
args.conclusion: a rift where the crust splits

heading: The first clue was a valley nobody expected
narration: Tharp argued it was a rift, a place where the crust was splitting.

heading: The first clue was a valley nobody expected
narration: Heezen was at first sceptical, because continental drift was then a minority view among geologists.

args.title: Mapping the Atlantic floor
args.conclusion: a rift where the crust splits

heading: The first clue was a valley nobody expected
narration: But the pattern held as more soundings came in, and it lined up with where earthquakes clustered beneath the ocean. A rift where the crust splits was the reading that survived.

heading: The first clue was a valley nobody expected
narration: A map, though, shows shape. It cannot show motion. A valley along a ridge is consistent with spreading, but it does not prove it.

heading: The first clue was a valley nobody expected
narration: For that, someone needed a way to read time off the seafloor itself.

heading: The seafloor recorded its own age in magnetism
narration: The key came from magnetism. When basalt cools at the ridge, iron-bearing minerals inside it align with Earth's magnetic field, and that alignment is fixed as the rock drops below what is called the Curie temperature.

args.title: Reading the magnetic stripes
steps: iron minerals lock in the field

heading: The seafloor recorded its own age in magnetism
narration: The iron minerals lock in the field as it was at that moment.

heading: The seafloor recorded its own age in magnetism
narration: And Earth's field does not stay put. Over geological time, the field reverses, with magnetic north and south swapping places.

args.title: Reading the magnetic stripes
steps: iron minerals lock in the field

heading: The seafloor recorded its own age in magnetism
narration: Ships towing magnetometers had already found long stripes of seafloor magnetised alternately one way and the other.

heading: The seafloor recorded its own age in magnetism
narration: Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews, and independently Lawrence Morley, proposed that the stripes mirror on both sides of a ridge because new crust forms at the centre and carries each reversal outward in both directions. In other words, the seafloor is spreading.

args.title: Reading the magnetic stripes

heading: The seafloor recorded its own age in magnetism
narration: Vine and Matthews published their argument in the journal Nature, and it turned an earlier hypothesis into something testable.

args.meaning: new crust forming at a ridge and moving away on both sides
args.boundary: it does not say what drives the plates

heading: The seafloor recorded its own age in magnetism
narration: Harry Hess had already proposed seafloor spreading: new crust forming at a ridge and moving away on both sides.

heading: The seafloor recorded its own age in magnetism
narration: The magnetic stripes were the record that idea predicted, a symmetrical tape running outward from the crest.

args.meaning: new crust forming at a ridge and moving away on both sides

narration: Notice what the idea did not explain on its own. It does not say what drives the plates.

heading: The seafloor recorded its own age in magnetism
narration: That part came later, and it is still being refined. That the seafloor spreads is one finding. Why it spreads is a separate question.

heading: Drilling and diving checked the prediction
narration: A good hypothesis sticks its neck out, and spreading made predictions that could have failed.

heading: Drilling and diving checked the prediction
narration: If the crust is born at the ridge, then sediment thickens away from the ridge, because older floor has had longer to collect the particles that drift down from above.

heading: Drilling and diving checked the prediction
narration: And the crust grows older away from the ridge. The drilling ship Glomar Challenger, working for the Deep Sea Drilling Project, recovered cores across the South Atlantic and found exactly that progression.

args.title: What spreading predicted
items: +crust grows older away from the ridge

heading: Drilling and diving checked the prediction
narration: The oldest sediment lying directly on the basalt got older with distance from the crest, on both sides.

heading: Drilling and diving checked the prediction
narration: The pattern fit. The question of what drives the plates stayed open.

items: +crust grows older away from the ridge

heading: Drilling and diving checked the prediction
narration: There was another prediction. If seawater seeps into hot, freshly made crust, it should be heated and pushed back out, with hot water venting at the crest.

args.caption: Hydrothermal vents found at the Galápagos Rift

heading: Drilling and diving checked the prediction
narration: In 1977, scientists diving in the submersible Alvin, operated by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, known as WHOI, found hydrothermal vents on the Galápagos Rift, a spreading centre in the eastern Pacific.

heading: Drilling and diving checked the prediction
narration: They expected hot water. They did not expect the dense communities of animals living around it.

args.caption: Hydrothermal vents found at the Galápagos Rift

heading: Drilling and diving checked the prediction
narration: The geology was confirmed, and the biology opened an entirely new field.

heading: Spreading speed shapes the ridge
narration: Not every ridge looks like the one Tharp drew. Speed matters. USGS describes spreading at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge as slow, on the order of a few centimetres a year, roughly the pace at which your fingernails grow.

heading: Spreading speed shapes the ridge
narration: Ridges that spread faster, such as the East Pacific Rise, receive magma more steadily.

heading: Spreading speed shapes the ridge
narration: A slow-spreading ridge tends to show a deep central rift valley, not a smooth central high.

heading: Spreading speed shapes the ridge
narration: Fast ridges show the reverse: a broad swell with little or no valley at its crest.

heading: Spreading speed shapes the ridge
narration: Exact rates differ along each ridge and between studies, so treat any single figure as an average over a long stretch of seafloor.

heading: Spreading speed shapes the ridge
narration: Fractures also break the ridge into offset segments. These transform faults, where the plates slide past each other sideways, are why the ridge zigzags on a map instead of running in one clean line.

heading: Spreading speed shapes the ridge
narration: And in one place the ridge rises above the waves. Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where an unusually generous magma supply, usually attributed to a mantle hotspot, has built the crest high enough to form land.

heading: Spreading speed shapes the ridge
narration: There you can stand inside a rift valley in open air and see the process the deep sea normally hides.

narration: Most of this story is told in mechanisms rather than figures, because the mechanism is what the evidence actually pins down.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Here is the edge of it. The evidence firmly establishes that new crust forms at ridges, and that the ridge is high because it is hot.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: It does not establish exactly how melt gathers beneath the crest: how it migrates upward through mostly solid rock and focuses into a narrow band at the axis is still modelled and argued over.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Nor does it settle how much each force drives the plates. Slab pull is widely judged the largest, but the balance between it and other forces is estimated, not measured directly.

args.title: What the evidence settles

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Most of the ridge has never been seen up close, and the mantle beneath it has never been sampled in place.

heading: Closing
narration: So ocean ridges are not pushed up. The longest mountain range on Earth is not a wall raised by collision but a seam that never finishes closing, built from rock that melted because the weight above it lifted, and that will sink again as it cools.

heading: Closing
narration: Every stretch of ocean floor began there, at a crest, as something briefly molten.
